title: Identifiers and C# Naming Rules
learningObjectives: Identify the lexical rules for valid C# identifiers.
Recognize reserved keywords and the verbatim identifier prefix @.
Apply common naming conventions for locals, fields and types.
Choose descriptive names that improve readability.

understand.concept: An identifier is a name used for a program element such as a variable, method, class or namespace. C# identifiers follow language rules, are case-sensitive and should follow established .NET naming conventions. Reserved keywords have special meaning unless escaped with the @ prefix.
understand.whyItMatters: Good identifiers make programs understandable and reduce mistakes. Consistent naming also helps teams navigate code and recognize the role of each program element.
understand.analogy: An identifier is like a person's name on a labelled record: it must follow the system's naming rules and should be distinct enough to avoid confusion.
understand.analogyLimit: Naming conventions are guidance, not all compiler-enforced rules. A name can compile and still be confusing or misleading.

explain.narrative:
## Identifier rules

A normal identifier starts with a letter or underscore and can continue with letters, decimal digits and other characters allowed by the language. It cannot start with a digit. C# supports Unicode identifier characters, but simple names are often easier to share across tools.

## Case sensitivity

C# treats score and Score as different identifiers. Avoid names that differ only by casing because they are easy to confuse.

## Keywords and @

Words such as class, int and return are reserved keywords. The @ prefix allows a keyword to be used as an identifier, for example @class. The @ symbol is not part of the identifier's stored name.

## Naming conventions

Use PascalCase for types and public members, camelCase for local variables and parameters, and meaningful names that describe purpose. Follow one consistent project convention for constants and private fields.

## Version baseline

Identifier rules are defined by the C# language. The examples compile with C# 14 and .NET 10.

examples.title: Use meaningful parameter names
examples.code:
static int CalculateTotal(int unitPrice, int quantity) => unitPrice * quantity;
Console.WriteLine(CalculateTotal(12, 5));
examples.explanation: The parameter names describe their roles and make the calculation easier to read.
